title: Second Normal Form (2NF)
description: Decompose enrollment facts into second normal form, prove the information-preserving split, and distinguish partial-key repairs from remaining instructor dependencies.

questions.question_text: Why is the original StudentCourse table NOT in 2NF?
options: Because it contains a comma-separated list
Because non-key attributes like StudentName and CourseName are only partially dependent on the composite key {StudentID, CourseID}, not fully dependent on the whole key
Because it lacks a primary key entirely
Because InstructorOffice is nullable
questions.explanation: 2NF requires every non-key attribute to be fully dependent on the whole key; here, StudentName depends on StudentID alone and CourseName on CourseID alone, both partial dependencies.

questions.question_text: Which decomposition correctly achieves 2NF for StudentCourse?
options: Merging all attributes into one wider table with more indexes
Student(StudentID, StudentName), Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice), Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollmentDate)
Simply removing the EnrollmentDate column
Sorting the table by StudentID
questions.explanation: Each partially-dependent attribute is relocated to a relation keyed by exactly the subset of the key it truly depends on, leaving only the fully-dependent EnrollmentDate with the composite key.

questions.question_text: If every candidate key is a singleton and no nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies apply, why is ordinary partial-key violation absent?
options: Singleton keys have no functional dependencies
No candidate key has a proper nonempty subset that can determine a nonprime attribute
2NF applies only above five columns
Singleton keys are always surrogate
questions.explanation: A singleton PRIMARY KEY alone is not enough if another composite candidate key exists. The all-key and empty-determinant assumptions scope the statement.

questions.question_text: After the 2NF decomposition, is the new Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) relation itself in 2NF?
options: No, because InstructorOffice still causes a partial dependency
Yes — CourseID is a single-attribute key here, so partial dependency is impossible; but it still has a transitive dependency issue that 2NF doesn't address
No, because it now has too many attributes
Yes, and it has no remaining design issues of any kind
questions.explanation: Under the stated dependencies CourseID is the only candidate key and no empty determinant applies, so the relation is 2NF. InstructorID still creates a transitive issue that later normalization addresses.

questions.question_text: Which anomaly from earlier topics does the 2NF decomposition directly fix regarding StudentName?
options: It has no effect on any anomaly
The redundancy of storing 'Asha' multiple times is fixed — StudentName is now stored once per student in the Student table regardless of how many courses she takes
It fixes the deletion anomaly for instructor data
It prevents students from enrolling in more than one course
questions.explanation: Once StudentName lives in its own Student(StudentID, StudentName) relation, it is stored exactly once per student, eliminating the redundancy caused by its earlier partial dependency.

questions.question_text: Does achieving 2NF fully eliminate the update anomaly for InstructorOffice (e.g., when Dr. Rao changes offices)?
options: Yes, 2NF fully resolves all anomalies related to instructors

No — InstructorOffice is still reached transitively through InstructorID within the Course table, so changing an instructor's office still requires updating every course row they teach, until 3NF fixes it
Yes, because InstructorOffice is now a foreign key
No, because 2NF only applies to StudentName
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependency, but the transitive chain CourseID -> InstructorID -> InstructorOffice remains inside the Course relation, so the update anomaly persists until 3NF's further decomposition.

questions.question_text: If a relation has two different candidate keys, how should 2NF be checked?
options: Only against whichever key is declared PRIMARY KEY in SQL
Against every candidate key — an attribute could be partially dependent on one candidate key even while fully dependent on another
2NF cannot be defined for relations with multiple candidate keys
Only against the candidate key with the most attributes
questions.explanation: 2NF's definition requires checking full/partial dependency against every candidate key of the relation, not just an arbitrarily chosen primary key.

questions.question_text: What is the precise formal definition of 2NF?
options: Every determinant must be a candidate key
The relation is 1NF and every nonprime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key
There are no multivalued dependencies
Every value is merely nonnull
questions.explanation: Use nonprime rather than an ambiguous non-key label, and inspect every candidate key.

questions.question_text: Which attributes does 2NF constrain relative to candidate keys?
options: Nonprime attributes
Only primary-key columns
Only nullable strings
Only foreign keys
questions.explanation: Nonprime means membership in no candidate key.

questions.question_text: Where belongs EnrollmentDate under the stated dependencies?
options: Student only
Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollmentDate)
Instructor only
An unrelated report label
questions.explanation: It describes the association and needs the whole pair.

questions.question_text: Does repeated StudentName in a joined report recreate stored redundancy?
options: Yes, all repeated displays violate 2NF
No, presentation repetition differs from duplicate authoritative storage
Only if sorted
Only for text
questions.explanation: One stored student fact can appear in several relationship-grain output rows.

questions.question_text: What justifies separating Student from the legal original relation?
options: Both table names begin with S
A report has two rows
Shared StudentID determines the Student component
A query uses DISTINCT
questions.explanation: The determinant supports a lossless decomposition argument.

questions.question_text: Can a composite-key association relation satisfy 2NF?
options: No, composite keys are forbidden
Only if empty
Only after adding a surrogate
Yes, when its nonprime facts need every candidate key fully
questions.explanation: The rule targets partial dependency, not composite keys themselves.

questions.question_text: Why can a surrogate EnrollmentID fail to fix the original violation?
options: The composite candidate key and its partial dependencies remain
The generated key cannot be unique
It automatically deletes course facts
Every surrogate violates 1NF
questions.explanation: All candidate keys matter, not only the chosen primary key.

questions.question_text: What remains redundant in the intermediate Course relation?
options: The student identifier in Student
Instructor facts shared across an instructor’s courses
The enrollment-specific date
Every course primary key
questions.explanation: 2NF does not remove every transitive dependency.

questions.question_text: Should conflicting source course titles be resolved by arbitrary MIN during real conversion?
options: Yes, it proves the dependency
Only when uppercase
No, reconcile the authoritative fact
Only with no foreign key
questions.explanation: A design assumption cannot silently resolve inconsistent operational data.

questions.question_text: What is a prime attribute?
options: An attribute whose value is always a prime number
Every chosen display name
Only a primary-key label
An attribute in at least one candidate key
questions.explanation: Prime classification depends on the complete candidate-key set.

questions.question_text: Under the stated model, why does CourseID identify the course component?
options: It determines every course-component attribute
Its name contains ID
It appears first in SELECT
It is always the smallest integer
questions.explanation: The declared dependency chain establishes its key role.

questions.question_text: What must a historical student-name snapshot have?
options: Automatic replacement by every current-name edit
A separately defined meaning and update policy
No relationship identity
The same unqualified meaning as current name
questions.explanation: Current facts and historical observations can legitimately differ.

questions.question_text: Does achieving 2NF prove the absence of all update anomalies?
options: Yes, by definition
Only for single-column keys
No
Only after COMMIT
questions.explanation: Later dependencies can still create redundancy and need further design.

notes:
## Store each fact at the grain that determines it

Second normal form, abbreviated 2NF, requires a relation in first normal form whose nonprime attributes are fully functionally dependent on every candidate key. A nonprime attribute belongs to no candidate key. Full dependency means no proper subset of the candidate key already determines that attribute. The definition checks every candidate key, rather than only the one declared PRIMARY KEY in a particular SQL table.

This rule addresses a common design mistake: storing facts about individual entities alongside facts about their relationship. An enrollment identifies a student-course association. A student's current name describes the student, and a course's current title describes the course. Repeating both descriptions in every enrollment creates dependencies at different grains inside one relation, even when each column contains a single ordinary value and the table already satisfies the intended first-normal-form representation.

## State the dependencies of the running relation

Use StudentCourse(StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice, EnrollmentDate). Assume StudentID determines StudentName; CourseID determines CourseName and InstructorID; InstructorID determines InstructorName and InstructorOffice; and StudentID, CourseID determines EnrollmentDate. The simplified domain permits one enrollment per student-course pair and one assigned instructor per course. Different institutional requirements would need a different key and dependency analysis.

The candidate key is StudentID, CourseID. Both identifiers are necessary because neither a student alone nor a course alone identifies an enrollment. Together they determine the enrollment date and all the descriptive attributes through the stated chains. StudentName depends on StudentID alone, while CourseName and the instructor attributes can be reached from CourseID alone. These nonprime attributes therefore do not need the whole enrollment key.

The relation is not in2NF under those assumptions. The problem is not that a name repeats or that a composite key exists. The problem is a nonprime attribute determined by a proper subset of a candidate key. A composite key with only genuinely association-specific nonprime facts can satisfy 2NF perfectly well. Conversely, a single-column chosen primary key can coexist with an alternative composite candidate key that still exposes a violation.

## Decompose the enrollment relation into three roles

Move student facts into Student(StudentID, StudentName). Move course and currently associated instructor facts into Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice). Retain Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollmentDate) for the student-course association. The intermediate course design is deliberately a2NF step; it still needs a later analysis of instructor dependencies rather than being presented as a final anomaly-free schema.

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (
  student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE courses (
  course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  course_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  instructor_id INT NOT NULL,
  instructor_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  instructor_office VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id INT NOT NULL,
  enrollment_date DATE NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY(student_id) REFERENCES students(student_id),
  FOREIGN KEY(course_id) REFERENCES courses(course_id)
);
```

The two foreign keys retain valid associations with existing students and courses. They do not copy the student name into each enrollment. StudentName is stored once per student, regardless of how many courses that student takes. CourseName is stored once per course, regardless of how many learners enroll. The enrollment date remains attached to the pair because it describes that particular relationship in the stated domain.

## Reconstruct the report without recreating stored redundancy

A report can join the three tables and display the same information as the original wide relation. Repetition in a query result is not the same as maintaining duplicate authoritative facts in storage. Seeing a course title beside every learner can be useful presentation. The design improvement concerns where the title is independently changed and enforced, not a prohibition on displaying it more than once.

```sql
SELECT e.student_id,s.student_name,e.course_id,c.course_name,
       e.enrollment_date
FROM enrollments e
JOIN students s ON s.student_id=e.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.course_id=e.course_id
ORDER BY e.student_id,e.course_id;
```

For student seven enrolled in courses four and six, the report has two rows with the same student name but different course identifiers and dates. That is expected result grain. Updating the one student record changes the current name used by both report rows. If the requirement instead preserves the name as recorded at enrollment, that historical snapshot needs an explicit separate meaning rather than being silently overwritten as though it were the current-name fact.

## Explain why the split preserves information

Under the declared dependencies, splitting student facts from the original relation is lossless because the shared StudentID determines the student component. Splitting course facts is similarly justified by CourseID determining the course component. Rejoining projections of a legal original state reconstructs the original enrollment facts without introducing spurious combinations. This is a dependency argument, not merely an observation that one small fixture happened to join correctly.

Migration of real data would first need to identify conflicts such as two current names for one student or two course titles for one course. Choosing an arbitrary MIN value would conceal the disagreement rather than resolve the authoritative fact. A teaching decomposition can assume a legal input relation; an operational conversion must validate and reconcile its actual input before enforcing the new structure. This lesson prepares the design reasoning and does not perform any migration.

## Know which anomaly remains in the course relation

An instructor can teach several courses under the stated assumptions. The intermediate Course relation therefore repeats InstructorName and InstructorOffice for every course assigned to that instructor. InstructorID determines these values without necessarily identifying one course. The relation can satisfy 2NF because its only candidate key is CourseID under the stated rules, while retaining a transitive nonkey dependency addressed by later normalization.

A change of office still requires coordinated updates across that instructor's course rows. Reaching 2NF has removed enrollment-level partial dependencies but has not removed every update anomaly. Third normal form would examine separating instructor facts into their own relation. Do not describe normal forms as a sequence of cosmetic table-count targets: each step follows a precise dependency and preserves an explicitly defined set of facts.

## Check alternative keys and empty determinants

If a surrogate EnrollmentID is added while the student-course pair remains a candidate key, the original wide relation does not automatically become 2NF. The nonprime course name still depends on CourseID alone, a proper subset of the alternative composite key. Inspect every minimal key before concluding that a generated identifier solved the design problem.

When every candidate key is a singleton and the model has no relevant nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies, ordinary partial-key violations are absent. The qualification about the empty set makes the statement precise: a constant attribute can be determined without any input attributes in a domain that requires that constant. Introductory examples often exclude that case, but a formal explanation should state its assumption rather than claim single attributes have no proper subset at all.

## Test the design through ordinary maintenance

Insert a student before that student chooses any course. The Student relation can represent the fact without inventing an enrollment date or a placeholder course. Likewise, a newly planned course can exist before anyone enrolls. Deleting the final Enrollment association does not remove either independently meaningful entity. These examples connect the dependency split to insertion and deletion behavior rather than leaving normalization as a vocabulary exercise.

Also test a legitimate name collision: two different students can both be named Asha while retaining different identifiers and enrollments. A join on StudentName would incorrectly combine their relationships. The decomposition must use the declared identifiers, preserve foreign-key meaning and specify its output grain. A result that merely looks plausible on a sample with unique names is insufficient evidence of a correct reconstruction.

## Solve two normalization decisions

First exercise: locate StudentName, CourseName and EnrollmentDate after the split. The solution places the first in Student, the second in Course and the third in Enrollment. Explain why removing duplicate enrollment rows by student would lose legitimate course associations. The goal is to relocate shared facts while preserving every valid relationship, including two students sharing a display name.

Second exercise: let instructor ten teach courses four and six with the same current office. Does the proposed 2NF schema eliminate the office-update anomaly? No: two Course rows still contain that shared instructor fact. Show a partial office update and explain the remaining inconsistency, then propose an Instructor relation as the next design step. Continue with [partial dependency](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/partial-dependency), [third normal form](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/3nf) and [BCNF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/bcnf) to keep the guarantees distinct.
